pairs.evidence: app/apply/[id]/candidate-door-conversion.test.ts:88 The usage claim 'Submit is BTN_PRIMARY' is checked with a bare identifier, and the import line that the previous assertion (line 87) requires already contains that name (ApplyFollowup.tsx:6 imports BTN_PRIMARY), so the pin stays green if the button stops using the recipe. quick-apply-status-link.test.ts:68 has the same flaw: StatusClient.tsx:8's import satisfies its LanguageSwitcher check.

techniques.evidence: app/apply/[id]/candidate-door-conversion.test.ts:88 Breaks the rule that the needle must carry a token prose cannot write. The name alone matches the import line, so the pin cannot fail while the import stays. The same file shows the right form: line 44 reads rendered className values only, and line 162 tolerates \r?\n.

app/apply/[id]/apply-draft-fingerprint.test.ts:12 The shared predicate's behaviour is unit-tested elsewhere, and this file pins its adoption at the call sites. The header (line 9) says this is a source-contract interim because the site cannot be reached in the unit runner.

app/apply/[id]/candidate-door-conversion.test.ts:112 The offending shape is seeded into a copy of the real source and the pin is shown to go red, which is how the technique proves a structural pin can fail.
app/apply/[id]/candidate-door-conversion.test.ts:45 The extracted class-name set has a floor, so if the slice stops matching anything the loop cannot pass with nothing checked.

pairs.registryProposal: pin-the-call-not-the-name states the import-line trap for ordering claims ('a bare identifier is never usable for an ordering claim'). The measured case here is a presence/usage claim, where the same import line satisfies a bare-name needle in the permissive direction. The decision rule could say outright that a usage claim needs a use-site token (an interpolation, a JSX tag, or a call), not just an ordering claim.
